lead: A thin flange or web in compression does not wait for the whole column to fail. Its flat plate element buckles locally at a stress set by b/t, then keeps carrying load in a new pattern until crippling. Crippling stress σcrip is the useful compression strength of a thin-walled section. Needham's empirical curves and Gerard's semi-empirical method estimate σcrip from b/t and material data. Designers use these charts for wing stringers, fuselage frames and stiffened panels, where weight matters and local failure often decides the section.
prereq: You need: 6.3 for plate buckling, 6.4 for effective width, and Unit 3 inelastic buckling for the yield cut-off.

blocks.text: Compression elements behave as plates. A flange attached to a web has one long edge supported and one long edge free. A web between flanges has both long edges supported. The flat width b is the clear width between supports or between a support and a free edge. Thickness is t. The ratio b/t is the main local buckling parameter.

blocks.where: σel is the elastic local buckling stress (Pa); k is the plate buckling coefficient: use k = 4.0 for a long plate with both long edges simply supported in compression (a web between flanges); use k ≈ 0.43 for a long plate with one long edge supported and one long edge free (a flange attached to a web). Choose k for the edge condition before computing σel; E is Young's modulus (Pa); ν is Poisson's ratio; b is flat width (m); t is thickness (m).

blocks.text: Thin aircraft sheet has high b/t, so σel can be well below σcy, the compressive yield stress. The element buckles locally, but the panel can still carry more load. The buckle shifts load to stiffer edges and membrane action develops. Final failure is crippling: local yielding and instability combine, and the element cannot carry extra compression. The crippling stress σcrip is the average compressive stress at crippling. When σel is below σcy, σcrip lies between σel and σcy. When σel is above σcy, the element yields before it buckles and σcrip is taken as σcy.

Needham's method is empirical. Needham tested thin-walled sections and plotted σcrip/σcy against b/t for each family: angle, channel, Z, hat, I. Each curve includes local buckling, post-buckling, corner restraint and yielding. Use the curve for the actual family. An angle curve does not apply to a channel.

The curve falls as b/t rises. At low b/t the ratio approaches 1. At high b/t it can be 0.3 or less. The physical cut-off is σcrip ≤ σcy. A chart reading above 1 means the element yields before it cripples; take σcy.

Gerard's method is semi-empirical. It correlates test data using the parameter (b/t)√(σcy/E), with a coefficient that depends on section shape and end conditions. The chart gives σcrip/σcy. The coefficient is not universal. Do not assume one universal formula; use the chart or coefficients supplied with the problem.

The section crippling load is Pcrip = σcrip A, where A is the total cross-sectional area of the thin-walled section (m²). Use the same units for stress and area. For a section with several flat elements, the largest b/t element is usually critical, but the chart for the whole section family is preferred.

sections.h3: Design procedure, inter-rivet buckling and wrinkling

items: Draw the section; mark supported and free edges.
Measure clear flat width b and thickness t for each element.
Compute b/t and the elastic local buckling stress σel.
Select the Needham curve or Gerard parameter for the section family.
Read σcrip/σcy; cap the ratio at 1.0.
Compute Pcrip = σcrip A; check inter-rivet p/t and sheet wrinkling.

blocks.text: Inter-rivet buckling is local buckling of sheet between rivets. The relevant width is rivet pitch p, not panel width b. Put p/t into the elastic plate formula. If p/t is large, sheet buckles between rivets and the rivets no longer support the skin. Reduce pitch or increase thickness.

Sheet wrinkling is short-wave buckling of thin skin restrained by stringers. It depends on skin thickness, stringer bending stiffness and attachment stiffness. It is not the same as general panel buckling. Check wrinkling allowables; it can set a lower stress than the section crippling chart.
For composite shapes, local buckling uses orthotropic plate stiffnesses; the empirical crippling charts are material-specific. See 6.7.

figure.caption: An angle crippling curve falls as b/t rises; the marked point is b/t=15 with ratio 0.60, and the flat line is the yield cut-off.

spec.aria: Plot of crippling stress ratio against b/t with an angle crippling curve falling as b/t rises, an example point at b/t 15 and ratio 0.60, plus a yield cut-off line at ratio 1.

examples.question: A 2024-T3 aluminium alloy angle has compressive yield σcy = 320 MPa, flat width-to-thickness ratio b/t = 15 and cross-sectional area A = 180 mm². The Gerard chart for this angle gives σcrip/σcy = 0.60. Find the crippling stress and the crippling load.
steps: Write the data with units: σcy = 320 MPa, b/t = 15, A = 180 mm², σcrip/σcy = 0.60.
Crippling load: Pcrip = σcrip A = 192 × 10⁶ Pa × 180 × 10⁻⁶ m².
Round to three significant figures: Pcrip = 34.6 kN.
examples.answer: The crippling stress is 192 MPa and the crippling load is 34.6 kN.
examples.check:
sigma_cy = 320.0
ratio = 0.60
A_mm2 = 180.0
sigma_crip = ratio * sigma_cy
A_m2 = A_mm2 * 1e-6
P_N = sigma_crip * 1e6 * A_m2
P_kN = P_N / 1000.0
print(sigma_crip)
print(round(P_kN, 1))

traps: Using the elastic local buckling stress σel as the crippling stress. Crippling includes post-local-buckling and yielding effects.
Forgetting the yield cut-off. A chart ratio above 1 is not allowed; σcrip cannot exceed σcy.
Using the wrong Needham curve or Gerard coefficient for the section family. An angle, channel and hat section have different curves.
Measuring b as the outer width instead of the clear flat width, or mixing free-edge and supported-edge cases.
Using panel width b where rivet pitch p is required for inter-rivet buckling, or mixing millimetres and metres in Pcrip = σcrip A.

quiz.a: σcrip is the average compressive stress at which a thin-walled section cripples by combined local yielding and instability, below or at compressive yield.

quiz.q: What does the ratio b/t mean in a thin compression element?
quiz.a: b is the clear flat width between supports or between a support and a free edge; t is the thickness. b/t controls local plate buckling.

quiz.q: Why can σcrip be lower than σcy for high b/t?
quiz.a: High b/t lowers the elastic local buckling stress. The element buckles locally and then fails by crippling through local yielding and instability before the whole section reaches yield.

quiz.q: Why must a Needham or Gerard chart reading be capped at σcrip/σcy = 1.0?
quiz.a: The compressive yield stress is an upper limit. If the chart predicts a higher stress, the material yields first; the cut-off is σcrip ≤ σcy.

quiz.q: An angle has σcy = 280 MPa, b/t = 20, A = 250 mm² and a chart ratio σcrip/σcy = 0.45. Find Pcrip.
A plate element has σel = 150 MPa and σcy = 300 MPa. Is σcrip equal to 150 MPa? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. σel is only the start of local buckling; σcrip is higher because post-buckling reserve carries more load, but it is capped at 300 MPa.

quiz.q: Two angles have the same area and σcy. One has b/t = 10 and the other b/t = 30. Which has the lower Pcrip, and why?
quiz.a: The b/t = 30 angle has lower Pcrip. Its larger b/t gives a lower chart ratio σcrip/σcy, so σcrip and Pcrip = σcrip A are lower.

quiz.q: Distinguish inter-rivet buckling from sheet wrinkling in a stiffened panel.
quiz.a: Inter-rivet buckling is local buckling of sheet between rivets, controlled by rivet pitch p and p/t. Sheet wrinkling is short-wave buckling of skin restrained by stringers, controlled by skin thickness, stringer stiffness and attachment stiffness. They are separate checks.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production stress offices keep crippling allowables as digital tables for each section family and material, and finite element models are checked against these charts. Composite crippling is an active research area because failure depends on ply stacking and defects. Search next for crippling allowable, Gerard method, inter-rivet buckling and sheet wrinkling.
